problem: Classical MPC navigation relies on hand-engineered cost functions. These fall into local minima, for example at doorways, and fail in tight clutter. They also cannot encode unwritten social norms, such as swinging wide at blind corners or keeping comfort distance from an obstructing pedestrian. End-to-end learned policies, in contrast, lack the safety and kinodynamic guarantees of MPC and generalize poorly. Standard Transformers are too slow (quadratic attention) to put inside a real-time MPC loop on a robot CPU.
motivation: Real-world deployment in homes and offices needs both near-collision maneuvering and socially compliant behavior. Cost functions for these are hard to design by hand, but a few expert demonstrations are easy to collect. MPC gives a strong inductive bias: constraints, dynamics and optimality. So learning only the cost, with visual context fed through an efficient attention model, could combine imitation learning's flexibility with MPC's robustness while keeping real-time speed on an onboard CPU.
key_idea: Augment an iLQR-based MPC's hand-designed cost with a context-dependent convex quadratic residual cost whose parameters (P, q) come from a low-rank linear-attention Performer over the occupancy grid. The Performer is trained end-to-end from demonstrations by differentiating through the MPC solution via the implicit function theorem (bilevel optimization).
insight: Keeping the learned part inside the MPC structure generalizes better than using the same Performer as an explicit policy that directly predicts a goal/reference state (EP). Evidence: in the unseen blind-corner, EP drops from 4.16 to 3.17 social score with a 20% failure rate, while Performer-MPC stays at 3.88/3.87 with 0% failures. On the real obstacle course EP (3/10 SR) is even worse than plain MPC (5/10), while Performer-MPC reaches 9/10. Two design choices make it work. First, the residual cost is quadratic in (x,u): this avoids re-quadratizing a large network in each iLQR iteration and keeps the cost convex and well-conditioned, so crude MPC solutions still give usable IFT gradients. Second, the speed ablation shows Performer-ReLU (no random features) is what makes on-robot use feasible: medium model 8.3 ms per MPC iteration versus 21.5–26.8 ms for Performer-Exp (67.6–81.6 ms with redraw). Performer-ReLU reaches near pixel-to-pixel (1×1 patch) attention at 11.3 ms CPU time per iteration.
method: Learnable MPC (inverse optimal control): at each step solve a T-horizon optimal control problem with differential-drive dynamics. The stagewise cost is c̄(x,u,t) + [x;u]^T P^T P [x;u] + q^T [x;u], where only the residual (P, q) is learned from context C0.

Hand-designed static cost c̄: asymmetric quartic forward/backward speed and turn-rate penalties, a ReLU² margin collision penalty on signed distances of body collision points, and a time-weighted goal position/orientation penalty.

Performer context encoder: a robot-frame occupancy grid (100×100 or 180×180, 0.05 m cells) goes through a conv patch embedding with positional encodings, then a 3-layer, 1-head, mlpdim=64 Performer-ReLU (linear attention via ReLU feature map, O(Lmd)). The final embedding of one token is de-vectorized into P and q.

Bilevel training via implicit differentiation: the outer loop minimizes imitation loss between MPC-generated and expert state/control trajectories. The gradient is a VJP combining an adjoint-method loss gradient with ∂θu* from the Implicit Function Theorem, computed as one extra TV-LQR solve after iLQR converges (trajax, 4 TPUs, ~0.36 s/iteration).
MPC solver: differentiable iLQR (Gauss-Newton with DDP-style line search), 20-step horizon and 20 iterations online, running on the robot CPU.

Tracking MPC: a secondary non-learnable MPC with only the static cost tracks an intermediate state from the learnable MPC's optimal trajectory to produce the final (v, ω) command. The same tracking layer is used for all baselines for fairness.

Distribution-shift mitigation and augmentation: recovery demos from 'disadvantage' or near-collision start states, random background shuffling of obstacle pixels (pedestrian obstruction), and randomized goal selection.

setting.backbone: 3-layer, 1-head Performer-ReLU (mlpdim 64) cost network trained from scratch + differentiable iLQR MPC (trajax)
setting.model_size: ~8.33M params (medium Performer-ReLU, 100×100 input, 5×5 patches); 15.7M with 1×1 patches
setting.training_data: Per-scenario expert demonstrations, one model per scenario. Doorway (sim): 2000 off-line iLQR+Dijkstra planner trajectories (100-horizon) windowed into 20-horizon snippets. Obstacle course: ~30 min human joystick teleop plus ~10 min recovery demos from failure locations. Social scenarios: ~30 human-teleoperated episodes each, with background-shuffling and random-goal augmentation for pedestrian obstruction.
setting.observation: robot-centric 2D occupancy grid from onboard SLAM (3D LiDAR + head depth sensors), 0.05 m cells, 100×100 (±2.5 m) or 180×180 (±4.5 m, pedestrian obstruction); plus robot pose and goal/waypoint
setting.action_space: continuous body-frame forward speed [-0.8, 0.8] m/s and turn rate [-1.2, 1.2] rad/s output by a tracking MPC (differential drive)
setting.simulator: unspecified 2D simulation for doorway traversal; the other three scenarios are real world only
setting.privileged: none (goal / coarse waypoints from a global planner on the SLAM map)

numbers_note: No standard embodied-navigation benchmarks are used. All four scenarios are custom (one simulated, three real-world) with small trial counts (10–100). Social results are pilot-study Likert averages, not statistically significant by the authors' own statement. Fig. 6 plots the same social scores as Tables 6–7. Train/test Hausdorff-loss curves appear only in Fig. 4. Speed ablations (e.g., medium Performer-ReLU 8.3 ms wall-clock per MPC iteration; 1×1 patch 11.3 ms CPU) are in Tables 1–4 and not listed as benchmark entries.
results: In the simulated doorway scenario Performer-MPC passes the doorway in 86/100 trials, versus 24/100 for a regular MPC (RMPC). On a real 4.5×10 m² cluttered obstacle course it gets 9/10 success and 92±6% completion, versus RMPC 5/10 (69±13%) and the Explicit Policy baseline 3/10 (62±15%). In real-world social pilot studies it scores 3.88/3.87 (seen/unseen) on blind corner and 4.39/4.10 on pedestrian obstruction with 0% failures. RMPC scores 1.88/2.38 and 1.55/1.96 on the same scenarios. EP matches or beats it in seen blind-corner (4.16) but degrades unseen (3.17, 20% failures), and it fails 5% of the time on pedestrian obstruction. All of this runs at real-time speed (8.3 ms per MPC iteration) on the onboard CPU.
limitations: Only spatial attention over a single occupancy-grid frame: there is no temporal history or human-motion prediction, and no richer modalities (RGB, language). Scenarios are limited to what the occupancy grid can express.
The quadratic residual cost limits expressiveness, and a separate cost is learned per scenario; it is unclear how one cost function would handle multiple scenarios.

Evaluation is small-scale: few trials, and the social study is a pilot with N=9 research-team members, unbalanced design, descriptive statistics only. One question (BC2) implicitly prescribed a behavior.
